questions.question: State the four assumptions of the PPC model and explain why every point on the curve is a maximum.
questions.expected_answer: The model assumes only two goods are produced, resources are fixed in quantity and quality, technology is fixed, and all resources are fully and efficiently employed. Because everything is already employed, each point on the curve shows the greatest amount of one good obtainable once the quantity of the other is chosen — more of one good can only be had by giving up some of the other, so no on-curve combination can be improved without a sacrifice.

questions.question: Using the wheat-and-wool schedule, explain what increasing opportunity cost means and why it makes the curve bow outward.
questions.expected_answer: Successive equal batches of wheat cost more and more wool: the first ten tonnes cost 2 bales, then 4, 7, 11 and 16. This is increasing opportunity cost. It happens because resources are not equally suited to both uses — the first paddocks switched to wheat are those best for grain, while later switches take land and labour that produced wool brilliantly but grow wheat poorly. Each extra tonne of wheat therefore costs more wool than the last, which bends the boundary outward rather than leaving it a straight line.

questions.question: Distinguish between a movement along the curve, a movement from inside toward the curve, and a shift of the curve — and state which one alone is economic growth.
questions.expected_answer: A movement along the curve is reallocation: a different mix of the two goods with unchanged capacity. A movement from an inside point toward the curve is recovery: idle resources being put back to work, producing more of everything with what always existed. A shift of the curve is a change in capacity itself — outward through more or better resources and technology, inward through destruction or loss. Only the outward shift of the curve is economic growth.
